content: Regular monitoring of blood pressure (BP) during pregnancy is essential for diagnosing and managing hypertensive disorders, such as pre-eclampsia. BP can be measured in various settings, including conventional clinics or through self-monitoring at home, and using different techniques, such as auscultatory or automated devices. Understanding how these settings and techniques influence maternal and perinatal outcomes, quality of life, and healthcare resource utilization is critical. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of BP measurement settings and techniques on outcomes in pregnant women. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving pregnant women, using validated BP devices in different settings or with different techniques. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by two authors, and the GRADE approach was used to evaluate the certainty of the evidence. Out of 21 identified studies, three RCTs were included, involving a total of 536,607 women. One of these studies was a large cluster-RCT with 536,233 deliveries, but it did not provide data for most of the outcomes of interest. The included studies were generally judged to have a low risk of bias, but the certainty of the evidence was low due to issues such as indirectness and imprecision. Meta-analysis was not feasible because each study examined different comparisons. None of the included studies reported the primary outcome of systolic BP ≥150 mmHg or important secondary outcomes such as antenatal hospital admissions, neonatal unit length of stay, or neonatal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Setting of BP Measurement: Self-Monitoring vs. Conventional Clinic Measurement One study involving 154 women compared self-monitoring of BP with conventional clinic measurement. No maternal deaths were reported in either group, and perinatal mortality was not reported. Self-monitoring may result in slightly more diagnoses of pre-eclampsia compared to usual care (risk ratio [RR] 1.49, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.87 to 2.54; low-certainty evidence), but the wide confidence interval suggests both potential benefit and harm. Self-monitoring may have little to no effect on the likelihood of labor induction (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.45; low-certainty evidence). The evidence is uncertain regarding the effects of self-monitoring on maternal intensive care unit (ICU) admission (RR 1.54, 95% CI 0.06 to 37.25; low-certainty evidence), stillbirth (RR 2.57, 95% CI 0.13 to 52.63; low-certainty evidence), neonatal death (RR 1.54, 95% CI 0.06 to 37.25; low-certainty evidence), or preterm birth (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.37 to 3.55; low-certainty evidence). Self-monitoring may lead to slightly more neonatal unit admissions compared to usual care (RR 1.53, 95% CI 0.65 to 3.62; low-certainty evidence), but the wide confidence interval includes the possibility of fewer admissions with self-monitoring. Technique of BP Measurement: Korotkoff Phase IV (K4) vs. Korotkoff Phase V (K5) One study involving 220 women compared the use of Korotkoff phase IV (K4, muffling sound) and Korotkoff phase V (K5, disappearance of sound) to measure diastolic BP. No maternal deaths were reported in either group. There may be little to no difference in the diagnosis of pre-eclampsia between the two techniques (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.49; low-certainty evidence), as the wide confidence interval includes the possibility of more diagnoses with K4. The evidence is uncertain regarding differences in perinatal mortality between the groups (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.16 to 7.92; low-certainty evidence). The study did not report data on maternal ICU admission, labor induction, stillbirth, neonatal death, preterm birth, or neonatal unit admissions. Technique of BP Measurement: CRADLE Device vs. Usual Care One large study involving 536,233 deliveries compared the use of the CRADLE device (a semi-automated BP monitor with additional features and an education package) with usual care. There may be little to no difference in maternal deaths between the two groups (adjusted RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.30 to 2.11; low-certainty evidence), but the confidence interval suggests both potential harm and benefit. The study did not report outcomes such as pre-eclampsia, labor induction, perinatal mortality, preterm birth, or neonatal unit admissions. Maternal ICU admission and perinatal outcomes (stillbirths and neonatal deaths) were only collected for a small subset of women, identified by an outcome rather than baseline characteristics, which compromised the randomization process. As a result, these data were not extracted. Authors' Conclusions The evidence regarding the benefits of self-monitoring BP in hypertensive pregnancies is limited and uncertain, based on a single feasibility study. Current practice supports the use of Korotkoff phase V (K5) for measuring diastolic BP in pregnant women with hypertension. The potential benefits of using the CRADLE device for BP measurement during pregnancy remain unclear due to limitations in the study design and data quality.
